questions.subject: databases
questions.question: In an entity–relationship diagram, a weak entity set is depicted by
options: a single rectangle.
a double rectangle.
a single diamond.
a double diamond.

solution.concept: ER notation. A weak entity set has no key attribute of its own; its existence depends on an owner entity set, so it is drawn as a double rectangle. Its identifying relationship is drawn as a double diamond, its partial key is underlined with a dashed line, and its total participation in the identifying relationship is shown by a double line.
steps: A weak entity set cannot be identified by its own attributes, only by (owner key + partial key).
The standard Chen notation distinguishes it with the double outline: double rectangle for the set, double diamond for the identifying relationship.
Hence the correct symbol for the weak entity set itself is the double rectangle.
solution.trap: Confusing the double rectangle (weak entity set) with the double diamond (identifying relationship). They are different symbols for different things and a question may ask for either.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. ER notation. A weak entity set has no key attribute of its own; its existence depends on an owner entity set, so it is drawn as a double rectangle. Its identifying relationship is drawn as a double diamond, its partial key is underlined with a dashed line, and its total participation in the identifying relationship is shown by a double line.

Step by step.

  1. A weak entity set cannot be identified by its own attributes, only by (owner key + partial key).
  2. The standard Chen notation distinguishes it with the double outline: double rectangle for the set, double diamond for the identifying relationship.
  3. Hence the correct symbol for the weak entity set itself is the double rectangle.

Answer: Option (B) — a double rectangle.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) A single rectangle denotes a strong (regular) entity set.
  • (C) A diamond denotes a relationship set, not an entity set.
  • (D) A double diamond denotes the identifying relationship of a weak entity set.

Common misconception. Confusing the double rectangle (weak entity set) with the double diamond (identifying relationship). They are different symbols for different things and a question may ask for either.

Faster method. If the option mentions a diamond at all, it is describing a relationship, not an entity set.

Takeaway. Fix the four ER symbols once: rectangle = entity set, double rectangle = weak entity set, diamond = relationship, double diamond = identifying relationship.

questions.question: Entity set A has a many-to-one relationship R with entity set B. The participation of A in R is total and the participation of B in R is partial. Which one of the following is necessarily TRUE?
options: Every entity of B is related to at least one entity of A.
Every entity of A is related to exactly one entity of B.
Every entity of B is related to exactly one entity of A.
R must be merged into B because B's participation is partial.

solution.concept: Cardinality ratio plus participation constraint. “Many-to-one from A to B” means each entity of A is related to at most one entity of B, while one entity of B may be related to many entities of A. Total participation of A adds “at least one”, and the two bounds together give “exactly one”.
steps: Many-to-one A → B: an A-entity can be linked to at most one B-entity.
Total participation of A: every A-entity is linked to at least one B-entity.
At most one and at least one give exactly one B-entity for every A-entity.
Partial participation of B only says some B-entities may have no A-entity at all; it constrains nothing about A.
solution.final: Option (B) — every entity of A is related to exactly one entity of B
solution.trap: Students read “partial participation of B” as if it weakened the constraint on A. Participation constrains only the entity set it is attached to.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Cardinality ratio plus participation constraint. “Many-to-one from A to B” means each entity of A is related to at most one entity of B, while one entity of B may be related to many entities of A. Total participation of A adds “at least one”, and the two bounds together give “exactly one”.

Step by step.

  1. Many-to-one A → B: an A-entity can be linked to at most one B-entity.
  2. Total participation of A: every A-entity is linked to at least one B-entity.
  3. At most one and at least one give exactly one B-entity for every A-entity.
  4. Partial participation of B only says some B-entities may have no A-entity at all; it constrains nothing about A.

Answer: Option (B) — every entity of A is related to exactly one entity of B.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) B's participation is partial, so a B-entity need not appear in R at all.
  • (C) Many-to-one allows many A-entities to share one B-entity, so B is not related to a unique A.
  • (D) A relationship is merged into an entity set only for a one-to-one or one-to-many case without loss, and partial participation of B does not force it.

Common misconception. Students read “partial participation of B” as if it weakened the constraint on A. Participation constrains only the entity set it is attached to.

Faster method. Total participation on the “many” side of a many-to-one turns “at most one” into “exactly one”.

Takeaway. Separate the two facts: the cardinality ratio bounds the count from above, participation bounds it from below. Combine them for the answer.

questions.question: In a Chen-notation ER diagram, which of the following are drawn with a double outline or a double diamond? (Select all that apply.)
options: A weak entity set.
The identifying relationship of a weak entity set.
A multivalued attribute.
A derived attribute.

solution.concept: ER notation distinguishes four special constructs. Double rectangle = weak entity set, double diamond = identifying relationship, double ellipse = multivalued attribute, dashed ellipse = derived attribute.
steps: (A) A weak entity set is drawn as a double rectangle — true.
(B) The identifying relationship is drawn as a double diamond — true.
(C) A multivalued attribute uses a double ellipse, not a double outline on a set or a relationship.
(D) A derived attribute uses a dashed ellipse.
solution.trap: The double ellipse for a multivalued attribute is confused with the double rectangle for a weak entity set. Both are “double”, but the shape differs and so does the meaning.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. ER notation distinguishes four special constructs. Double rectangle = weak entity set, double diamond = identifying relationship, double ellipse = multivalued attribute, dashed ellipse = derived attribute.

Step by step.

  1. (A) A weak entity set is drawn as a double rectangle — true.
  2. (B) The identifying relationship is drawn as a double diamond — true.
  3. (C) A multivalued attribute uses a double ellipse, not a double outline on a set or a relationship.
  4. (D) A derived attribute uses a dashed ellipse.

Answer: Options (A) and (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (C) uses a double ellipse, which is a different shape.
  • (D) uses a dashed ellipse.

Common misconception. The double ellipse for a multivalued attribute is confused with the double rectangle for a weak entity set. Both are “double”, but the shape differs and so does the meaning.

Takeaway. Remember the pairing shape-to-meaning: double rectangle / double diamond belong together as the weak-entity pair; double ellipse is an attribute-level symbol.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question:
Entity set E owns weak entity set W through an identifying relationship R. E has 4 entities, R permits at most 3 W-entities per E-entity, and every E-entity participates totally in R. What is the maximum possible number of entities in W?
(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: A weak entity set's cardinality is bounded by the owner's cardinality times the per-owner limit. Total participation of the owner gives a lower bound, the per-owner limit gives the upper bound.
steps: Every E-entity must own at least one W-entity (total participation), so |W| ≥ 4.
Each E-entity may own at most 3 W-entities, so |W| ≤ 4 × 3 = 12.
The upper bound 12 is attained when all 4 E-entities own the full 3 W-entities each.
So the maximum is 12.
solution.trap: Adding the two numbers instead of multiplying, or forgetting that a weak entity is owned by exactly one owner — which is what makes the count a product rather than a sum.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A weak entity set's cardinality is bounded by the owner's cardinality times the per-owner limit. Total participation of the owner gives a lower bound, the per-owner limit gives the upper bound.

Step by step.

  1. Every E-entity must own at least one W-entity (total participation), so |W| ≥ 4.
  2. Each E-entity may own at most 3 W-entities, so |W| ≤ 4 × 3 = 12.
  3. The upper bound 12 is attained when all 4 E-entities own the full 3 W-entities each.
  4. So the maximum is 12.

Answer: 12.

Common misconception. Adding the two numbers instead of multiplying, or forgetting that a weak entity is owned by exactly one owner — which is what makes the count a product rather than a sum.

Takeaway. For an identifying relationship the owner side is one-to-many, so multiply the owner count by the per-owner limit; the owner's participation decides the minimum, the limit decides the maximum.

questions.question: In ER modelling, aggregation is used to
options: combine several attributes of one entity set into a single composite attribute.
treat a relationship set together with its participating entity sets as one higher-level entity set that can then take part in another relationship.
replace a weak entity set by a strong entity set.
convert a ternary relationship into three binary relationships.

solution.concept: Aggregation is the ER construct that removes a limitation of plain ER diagrams: a relationship set cannot participate in another relationship. Aggregating a relationship plus its entity sets yields a single abstract entity that can.
steps: Plain ER forbids a relationship set from being an endpoint of another relationship.
Example: a project is done by employees using machines. “Uses” relates the (employee, project) pair to a machine, not an employee to a machine directly.
Aggregation groups Employee–Works_On–Project into one entity set and lets that set participate in Uses.
So aggregation abstracts a relationship together with its participants into a higher-level entity set.
solution.trap: Aggregation is confused with generalization (which factors common attributes of entity sets into a superclass) and with the composite-attribute notation. All three “combine” things, but at different levels.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Aggregation is the ER construct that removes a limitation of plain ER diagrams: a relationship set cannot participate in another relationship. Aggregating a relationship plus its entity sets yields a single abstract entity that can.

Step by step.

  1. Plain ER forbids a relationship set from being an endpoint of another relationship.
  2. Example: a project is done by employees using machines. “Uses” relates the (employee, project) pair to a machine, not an employee to a machine directly.
  3. Aggregation groups Employee–Works_On–Project into one entity set and lets that set participate in Uses.
  4. So aggregation abstracts a relationship together with its participants into a higher-level entity set.

Answer: Option (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) describes a composite attribute, drawn as an ellipse with sub-ellipses.
  • (C) is not an ER operation at all; a weak entity set stays weak unless the schema is redesigned.
  • (D) is a modelling decision about arity, not aggregation.

Common misconception. Aggregation is confused with generalization (which factors common attributes of entity sets into a superclass) and with the composite-attribute notation. All three “combine” things, but at different levels.

Faster method. If the sentence mentions “a relationship participating in another relationship”, the answer is aggregation.

Takeaway. Aggregation = relationship-as-entity. Generalization = entity-as-subclass. Composite attribute = attribute-of-attribute.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: A multivalued attribute in an ER diagram is represented by
options: a single ellipse.
a double ellipse.
a dashed ellipse.
a rectangle.

solution.concept: Attribute notation in Chen's model. A multivalued attribute can hold a set of values for one entity, and is drawn as a double ellipse. A derived attribute is drawn with a dashed ellipse; a key attribute has its name underlined.
steps: Multivalued means several values per entity, e.g. phone numbers of a person.
The extra value needs an extra outline, so the symbol is the double ellipse.
A derived attribute (computed from others, e.g. age from date of birth) uses a dashed ellipse instead.
solution.trap: The double ellipse is confused with the double rectangle of a weak entity set. Note that the doubling pattern is applied to the base shape: rectangle for sets, ellipse for attributes.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Attribute notation in Chen's model. A multivalued attribute can hold a set of values for one entity, and is drawn as a double ellipse. A derived attribute is drawn with a dashed ellipse; a key attribute has its name underlined.

Step by step.

  1. Multivalued means several values per entity, e.g. phone numbers of a person.
  2. The extra value needs an extra outline, so the symbol is the double ellipse.
  3. A derived attribute (computed from others, e.g. age from date of birth) uses a dashed ellipse instead.

Answer: Option (B) — a double ellipse.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) A single ellipse is a simple, single-valued attribute.
  • (C) A dashed ellipse is a derived attribute.
  • (D) A rectangle is an entity set.

Common misconception. The double ellipse is confused with the double rectangle of a weak entity set. Note that the doubling pattern is applied to the base shape: rectangle for sets, ellipse for attributes.

Takeaway. Learn the four attribute shapes together: single ellipse (simple), double ellipse (multivalued), dashed ellipse (derived), underlined name (key).

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: Relation R(A, B, C) has primary key (A, B) and a foreign key C that references S(C). Which one of the following is TRUE?
options: A and B cannot be NULL, but C may be NULL.
C cannot be NULL, but A may be NULL.
Any of A, B, C may be NULL.
A alone must be unique.

solution.concept: Entity integrity says no attribute of a primary key may be NULL; referential integrity says a foreign key must either be NULL or match an existing referenced value. The two rules apply to different attributes here, so both can hold at once.
steps: Entity integrity: every attribute of the primary key (A, B) is NOT NULL. So A and B cannot be NULL.
Referential integrity constrains C: each C-value must be NULL or equal some S.C value.
Nothing forbids C from being NULL, because C is not part of R's primary key.
Hence (A, B) are mandatory, C is optional.
solution.trap: Students assume a foreign key can never be NULL. It can, provided the FK attributes are not part of the primary key — that is exactly how “optional” relationships are modelled.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Entity integrity says no attribute of a primary key may be NULL; referential integrity says a foreign key must either be NULL or match an existing referenced value. The two rules apply to different attributes here, so both can hold at once.

Step by step.

  1. Entity integrity: every attribute of the primary key (A, B) is NOT NULL. So A and B cannot be NULL.
  2. Referential integrity constrains C: each C-value must be NULL or equal some S.C value.
  3. Nothing forbids C from being NULL, because C is not part of R's primary key.
  4. Hence (A, B) are mandatory, C is optional.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) reverses the two rules.
  • (C) contradicts entity integrity.
  • (D) A is only part of the key; A alone may repeat.

Common misconception. Students assume a foreign key can never be NULL. It can, provided the FK attributes are not part of the primary key — that is exactly how “optional” relationships are modelled.

Takeaway. Check whether the FK overlaps the primary key. No overlap → NULL is allowed. Overlap → entity integrity forbids NULL.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: Let R(A, B, C, D) satisfy the functional dependencies {AB → C, C → D, D → A}. How many candidate keys does R have?

solution.concept: A candidate key is a minimal set of attributes whose closure is the whole relation. Compute closures of each attribute alone, then of the promising pairs.
steps: A⁺ = A; B⁺ = B; C⁺ = C D A = ACD (using C → D and D → A); D⁺ = D A = AD. None is the whole relation.
AB⁺ = A B C D = ABCD. AB is a key, and neither A nor B alone is, so AB is a candidate key.
BC⁺ = B C D A = ABCD. BC is minimal (B⁺, C⁺ both fail), so BC is a candidate key.
BD⁺ = B D A = ABD, and AB → C applies, so BD⁺ = ABCD. BD is minimal, so BD is a candidate key.
AC⁺ = ACD, AD⁺ = AD, CD⁺ = ACD — none is the whole relation. The answer is 3.
solution.trap: Stopping at AB, or counting AB and BA as different keys. Also easy to miss BD, which needs the two-step closure D → A followed by AB → C.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A candidate key is a minimal set of attributes whose closure is the whole relation. Compute closures of each attribute alone, then of the promising pairs.

Step by step.

  1. A⁺ = A; B⁺ = B; C⁺ = C D A = ACD (using C → D and D → A); D⁺ = D A = AD. None is the whole relation.
  2. AB⁺ = A B C D = ABCD. AB is a key, and neither A nor B alone is, so AB is a candidate key.
  3. BC⁺ = B C D A = ABCD. BC is minimal (B⁺, C⁺ both fail), so BC is a candidate key.
  4. BD⁺ = B D A = ABD, and AB → C applies, so BD⁺ = ABCD. BD is minimal, so BD is a candidate key.
  5. AC⁺ = ACD, AD⁺ = AD, CD⁺ = ACD — none is the whole relation. The answer is 3.

Answer: Option (C) — 3 candidate keys (AB, BC, BD).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) misses BC and BD.
  • (B) misses BD.
  • (D) over-counts; AC, AD and CD are not keys.

Common misconception. Stopping at AB, or counting AB and BA as different keys. Also easy to miss BD, which needs the two-step closure D → A followed by AB → C.

Faster method. Here C and D never appear in a closure that contains B, so B is in every key. That forces you to test AB, BC and BD — exactly three.

Takeaway. Write every single-attribute closure first. Any attribute absent from all of them must appear in every candidate key; then test the minimal pairs containing it.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: Which of the following statements about keys of a relation are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Every relation has at least one candidate key.
A superkey that has no proper subset which is also a superkey is a candidate key.
A relation can have at most one candidate key.
A primary key attribute may contain NULL values.

solution.concept: Keys are defined through functional determination on the whole set of attributes. The set of all attributes of a relation is always a superkey, so minimal superkeys always exist.
steps: The full attribute set functionally determines itself, so it is a superkey; shrinking it until it is minimal yields a candidate key. Hence at least one candidate key always exists.
A candidate key is precisely a minimal superkey — that is the definition given in (B).
A relation may have several candidate keys; one of them is chosen as the primary key.
Entity integrity forbids NULL in any primary key attribute.
solution.trap: The word “candidate” is read as “optional”, suggesting there might be none. Every relation has at least one; what varies is how many.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Keys are defined through functional determination on the whole set of attributes. The set of all attributes of a relation is always a superkey, so minimal superkeys always exist.

Step by step.

  1. The full attribute set functionally determines itself, so it is a superkey; shrinking it until it is minimal yields a candidate key. Hence at least one candidate key always exists.
  2. A candidate key is precisely a minimal superkey — that is the definition given in (B).
  3. A relation may have several candidate keys; one of them is chosen as the primary key.
  4. Entity integrity forbids NULL in any primary key attribute.

Answer: Options (A) and (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (C) is false — a relation may have several candidate keys, and exactly one is picked as primary.
  • (D) is false — entity integrity requires primary key attributes to be NOT NULL.

Common misconception. The word “candidate” is read as “optional”, suggesting there might be none. Every relation has at least one; what varies is how many.

Takeaway. Two facts to keep: the full attribute set is always a superkey (so keys exist), and minimality is what separates candidate keys from superkeys.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question:
Relation R(A, B, C) satisfies the functional dependency A → B and no other non-trivial dependency. How many superkeys does R have?
(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: A superkey is any attribute set whose closure is all of R. With only A → B, the closure of a set S is S ∪ {B} if A ∈ S, and S otherwise; a superkey must therefore contain A and C.
steps: The candidate key: A⁺ = AB, so A alone is not a key; AC⁺ = ABC. Hence AC is the only candidate key.
Every superkey must contain the candidate key AC.
The only attributes available to add are the remaining ones, here just B, giving the supersets AC and ABC.
So R has exactly 2 superkeys.
solution.trap: Counting only AC and forgetting that a superkey may contain extra attributes, or counting A and C separately as keys.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A superkey is any attribute set whose closure is all of R. With only A → B, the closure of a set S is S ∪ {B} if A ∈ S, and S otherwise; a superkey must therefore contain A and C.

Step by step.

  1. The candidate key: A⁺ = AB, so A alone is not a key; AC⁺ = ABC. Hence AC is the only candidate key.
  2. Every superkey must contain the candidate key AC.
  3. The only attributes available to add are the remaining ones, here just B, giving the supersets AC and ABC.
  4. So R has exactly 2 superkeys.

Answer: 2.

Common misconception. Counting only AC and forgetting that a superkey may contain extra attributes, or counting A and C separately as keys.

Takeaway. Find the candidate key first; every superkey is then a superset of it, so the count is 2 raised to the number of leftover attributes.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: Let R(A, B, C, D, E) satisfy the functional dependencies {A → BC, CD → E, B → D, E → A}. How many candidate keys does R have?

solution.concept: Candidate keys are minimal sets with full closure. Because the dependencies form a cycle (A → B → D → E → A together with C on one edge), the relation has several minimal keys and every attribute belongs to at least one of them.
steps: A⁺: A → BC gives B, C; B → D gives D; CD → E gives E. So A⁺ = ABCDE. A is a candidate key.
E⁺: E → A, then A → BC, then B → D, then CD → E. So E⁺ = ABCDE. E is a candidate key.
BC⁺: B → D, CD → E, E → A, A → BC. So BC⁺ = ABCDE, and B⁺ = BD, C⁺ = C — BC is minimal.
CD⁺: CD → E, E → A, A → BC, B → D. So CD⁺ = ABCDE, and C⁺ = C, D⁺ = D — CD is minimal.
B⁺ = BD, C⁺ = C, D⁺ = D, BD⁺ = BD — none is the whole relation, and every other set contains one of A, E, BC, CD. So there are exactly 4 candidate keys.
solution.final: Option (C) — 4 candidate keys (A, E, BC, CD)
solution.trap: Missing E or CD because the cycle makes closure look “too easy”. The dependency cycle A → B → D → E → A means closure from any member reaches all the others, so several attributes become keys in their own right.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Candidate keys are minimal sets with full closure. Because the dependencies form a cycle (A → B → D → E → A together with C on one edge), the relation has several minimal keys and every attribute belongs to at least one of them.

Step by step.

  1. A⁺: A → BC gives B, C; B → D gives D; CD → E gives E. So A⁺ = ABCDE. A is a candidate key.
  2. E⁺: E → A, then A → BC, then B → D, then CD → E. So E⁺ = ABCDE. E is a candidate key.
  3. BC⁺: B → D, CD → E, E → A, A → BC. So BC⁺ = ABCDE, and B⁺ = BD, C⁺ = C — BC is minimal.
  4. CD⁺: CD → E, E → A, A → BC, B → D. So CD⁺ = ABCDE, and C⁺ = C, D⁺ = D — CD is minimal.
  5. B⁺ = BD, C⁺ = C, D⁺ = D, BD⁺ = BD — none is the whole relation, and every other set contains one of A, E, BC, CD. So there are exactly 4 candidate keys.

Answer: Option (C) — 4 candidate keys (A, E, BC, CD).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) misses BC and CD.
  • (B) misses one of E, BC, CD.
  • (D) over-counts: BD⁺ = BD is not a key.

Common misconception. Missing E or CD because the cycle makes closure look “too easy”. The dependency cycle A → B → D → E → A means closure from any member reaches all the others, so several attributes become keys in their own right.

Faster method. Any attribute whose single-attribute closure is the whole relation is a key by itself; here that is true of A and E, and the C-bearing pairs add two more.

Takeaway. When FDs form a cycle, compute closure from each single attribute first — every attribute that closes to ABCDE is already a key and needs no partner.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: Relation R(A, B) has A as its primary key and B as an ordinary nullable attribute. Which one of the following tuples, if inserted into R, violates a constraint implied by this schema?
options: (NULL, 5)
(1, NULL)
(1, 5)
(2, NULL)

solution.concept: Entity integrity: no component of a primary key may be NULL. B is not part of the key, so NULL is allowed there and only uniqueness would ever reject it — and NULLs do not clash with each other under this rule.
steps: A is the primary key, so every tuple must supply a non-NULL value for A.
(NULL, 5) supplies no key value, so it violates entity integrity.
(1, NULL) and (2, NULL) are fine: the key values 1 and 2 are present, B is nullable.
(1, 5) is fine as long as 1 is not already present.
solution.trap: Students reject (1, NULL) thinking no attribute may be NULL. Nullability is a schema property; only primary-key attributes are forced to be non-NULL.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Entity integrity: no component of a primary key may be NULL. B is not part of the key, so NULL is allowed there and only uniqueness would ever reject it — and NULLs do not clash with each other under this rule.

Step by step.

  1. A is the primary key, so every tuple must supply a non-NULL value for A.
  2. (NULL, 5) supplies no key value, so it violates entity integrity.
  3. (1, NULL) and (2, NULL) are fine: the key values 1 and 2 are present, B is nullable.
  4. (1, 5) is fine as long as 1 is not already present.

Answer: Option (A) — (NULL, 5).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) and (D) have a valid key value and a NULL in a nullable column.
  • (C) has a valid key value and no NULL.

Common misconception. Students reject (1, NULL) thinking no attribute may be NULL. Nullability is a schema property; only primary-key attributes are forced to be non-NULL.

Takeaway. Look at where NULL sits. Inside the primary key → rejected. Outside it → allowed unless the column is declared NOT NULL.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: In relational algebra, the division operator R ÷ S is used to express
options: universal quantification — the “for all” condition.
aggregation of a numeric attribute over groups.
an outer join that preserves unmatched tuples.
elimination of duplicates from a bag.

solution.concept: Division is the relational-algebra counterpart of universal quantification. R ÷ S keeps those A-values of R(A, B) that are paired in R with every B-value appearing in S.
steps: Write R(A, B) and S(B). R ÷ S = { a | for every b ∈ S, (a, b) ∈ R }.
The “for every b ∈ S” is exactly a ∀ condition, so division expresses queries such as “students who took all courses”.
It is not primitive: R ÷ S = π_A(R) − π_A( (π_A(R) × S) − R ).
solution.trap: Division is mistaken for ordinary arithmetic division or for a join. It answers “for all”, not “how many”.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Division is the relational-algebra counterpart of universal quantification. R ÷ S keeps those A-values of R(A, B) that are paired in R with every B-value appearing in S.

Step by step.

  1. Write R(A, B) and S(B). R ÷ S = { a | for every b ∈ S, (a, b) ∈ R }.
  2. The “for every b ∈ S” is exactly a ∀ condition, so division expresses queries such as “students who took all courses”.
  3. It is not primitive: R ÷ S = π_A(R) − π_A( (π_A(R) × S) − R ).

Answer: Option (A) — universal quantification.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) Aggregation is not an operator of the basic algebra at all; it is added as γ in extended algebra.
  • (C) Outer joins are extensions of ⋈, written ⟕ / ⟖ / ⟗.
  • (D) Duplicate elimination is implicit in every algebra operator, not the job of ÷.

Common misconception. Division is mistaken for ordinary arithmetic division or for a join. It answers “for all”, not “how many”.

Takeaway. Read division as a nested quantifier: keep a only if nothing in S is missing from a's row.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: Let R(A, B) = {(1, 10), (2, 20), (3, 10)} and S(B, C) = {(10, p), (20, q), (30, r)}. How many tuples are there in R ⋈ S (natural join)?

solution.concept: A natural join equates the common attribute B and concatenates matching pairs. Its size is Σ_b r_b · s_b over the common values, where r_b and s_b are the multiplicities of b in R and S.
steps: Common attribute is B.
B = 10 appears once in R and once in S → 1 × 1 = 1 tuple: (1, 10, p).
B = 20 appears once in R and once in S → 1 tuple: (2, 20, q).
B = 30 appears only in S → contributes nothing; B = 10 also occurs twice in R, so (3, 10, p) is a second tuple for B = 10.
Total = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3 tuples.
solution.trap: Students assume one output tuple per distinct value of B (giving 2), forgetting that repeated B values in R each match. The join is a cross product restricted to equal B.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A natural join equates the common attribute B and concatenates matching pairs. Its size is Σ_b r_b · s_b over the common values, where r_b and s_b are the multiplicities of b in R and S.

Step by step.

  1. Common attribute is B.
  2. B = 10 appears once in R and once in S → 1 × 1 = 1 tuple: (1, 10, p).
  3. B = 20 appears once in R and once in S → 1 tuple: (2, 20, q).
  4. B = 30 appears only in S → contributes nothing; B = 10 also occurs twice in R, so (3, 10, p) is a second tuple for B = 10.
  5. Total = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3 tuples.

Answer: Option (B) — 3 tuples.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) counts distinct B values instead of tuples.
  • (C) and (D) invent matches for B = 30, which is absent from R.

Common misconception. Students assume one output tuple per distinct value of B (giving 2), forgetting that repeated B values in R each match. The join is a cross product restricted to equal B.

Takeaway. Count multiplicities: for each common value b, multiply its count in R by its count in S and sum. Here 1·1 + 1·1 = 2 for B = 10 and B = 20, plus the second B = 10 row, giving 3.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: Which of the following statements about relational algebra operators are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Selection σ filters tuples and projection π filters attributes.
Projection π removes duplicate tuples from its result.
R − S and S − R are always equal.
R ∪ S is defined only when R and S are union-compatible.

solution.concept: Relational algebra is set-based, so every operator produces a relation, i.e. a set with no duplicate tuples, and the binary set operators require matching schemas.
steps: (A) σ keeps rows satisfying a predicate, π keeps a chosen list of columns — true.
(B) Because the result is a relation (a set), π collapses duplicates — true.
(C) Set difference is not symmetric: R − S keeps R's tuples absent from S, which is a different set from S − R.
(D) Union requires the same number of attributes with compatible domains in the same order — true.
solution.trap: The duplicate elimination of π is the usual surprise: SQL's SELECT does not remove duplicates, but relational algebra's π does. Mixing the two semantics is a standard error.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Relational algebra is set-based, so every operator produces a relation, i.e. a set with no duplicate tuples, and the binary set operators require matching schemas.

Step by step.

  1. (A) σ keeps rows satisfying a predicate, π keeps a chosen list of columns — true.
  2. (B) Because the result is a relation (a set), π collapses duplicates — true.
  3. (C) Set difference is not symmetric: R − S keeps R's tuples absent from S, which is a different set from S − R.
  4. (D) Union requires the same number of attributes with compatible domains in the same order — true.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (C) fails whenever the two relations are not identical: {1} − {2} = {1} but {2} − {1} = {2}.

Common misconception. The duplicate elimination of π is the usual surprise: SQL's SELECT does not remove duplicates, but relational algebra's π does. Mixing the two semantics is a standard error.

Takeaway. Remember: algebra = sets, SQL = bags. Every algebra operator, including π, returns a set.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question:
Let R(A, B) = {(a₁, b₁), (a₁, b₂), (a₂, b₁), (a₃, b₁), (a₃, b₂), (a₄, b₃)} and S(B) = {b₁, b₂}. How many tuples does R ÷ S contain?
(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: R ÷ S keeps an A-value only if it is paired with every B-value of S in R. Check each A-value against the full set {b₁, b₂}.
steps: a₁ is paired with b₁ and with b₂ → qualifies.
a₂ is paired only with b₁ → does not qualify.
a₃ is paired with b₁ and with b₂ → qualifies.
a₄ is paired only with b₃, which is not even in S → does not qualify.
So R ÷ S = {a₁, a₃}, two tuples.
solution.trap: Requiring only “at least one” match, which would keep a₂ and a₄ as well. Division demands every value of S, not any one of them.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. R ÷ S keeps an A-value only if it is paired with every B-value of S in R. Check each A-value against the full set {b₁, b₂}.

Step by step.

  1. a₁ is paired with b₁ and with b₂ → qualifies.
  2. a₂ is paired only with b₁ → does not qualify.
  3. a₃ is paired with b₁ and with b₂ → qualifies.
  4. a₄ is paired only with b₃, which is not even in S → does not qualify.
  5. So R ÷ S = {a₁, a₃}, two tuples.

Answer: 2.

Common misconception. Requiring only “at least one” match, which would keep a₂ and a₄ as well. Division demands every value of S, not any one of them.

Takeaway. Group R by A and check set-equality against S. Here a₁ and a₃ both map to exactly {b₁, b₂}.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question:
Consider the schema Doctor(did, dname, dage) and Patient(pid, rdid, pname, page), where rdid is a foreign key referencing did. Assume every doctor has at least one patient. Consider the relational algebra query
π_did(Doctor) − π_did( Doctor ⋈(did = rdid) ∧ (dage ≤ page) Patient )
The query evaluates to the set of dids of doctors whose age is greater than that of
options: some patient.
all patients.
some of his/her patients.
all of his/her patients.

solution.concept: Read the query as a set difference: start from all doctors, then remove the doctors that have a patient whose age is at least the doctor's. What survives is exactly the doctors for whom no such patient exists.
steps: Doctor ⋈<sub>(did = rdid) ∧ (dage ≤ page)</sub> Patient keeps pairs where the doctor's age is ≤ some patient's age, i.e. the doctor is not older than that patient.
Projecting on did gives the doctors having at least one patient who is at least as old as they are.
Subtracting this from π_did(Doctor) leaves the doctors who have no such patient.
“No patient is at least as old as the doctor” means the doctor is strictly older than every patient — all of his/her patients.
The assumption that every doctor has at least one patient matters: without it, a doctor with no patients would also survive, and the query would not mean “older than all”.
solution.trap: Answering “some patient” by stopping at the join instead of completing the difference, or reading the join's ≤ as if it removed patients rather than doctors.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Read the query as a set difference: start from all doctors, then remove the doctors that have a patient whose age is at least the doctor's. What survives is exactly the doctors for whom no such patient exists.

Step by step.

  1. Doctor ⋈(did = rdid) ∧ (dage ≤ page) Patient keeps pairs where the doctor's age is ≤ some patient's age, i.e. the doctor is not older than that patient.
  2. Projecting on did gives the doctors having at least one patient who is at least as old as they are.
  3. Subtracting this from π_did(Doctor) leaves the doctors who have no such patient.
  4. “No patient is at least as old as the doctor” means the doctor is strictly older than every patient — all of his/her patients.
  5. The assumption that every doctor has at least one patient matters: without it, a doctor with no patients would also survive, and the query would not mean “older than all”.

Answer: Option (D) — all of his/her patients.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) and (C) describe the set that is removed, not the set that survives.
  • (B) would require a ∀ condition expressed with division, not a single join.

Common misconception. Answering “some patient” by stopping at the join instead of completing the difference, or reading the join's ≤ as if it removed patients rather than doctors.

Faster method. Any “−” over a join that encodes “exists a violating tuple” is the standard pattern for a universal statement: removing the violators leaves the ones that satisfy “for all”.

Takeaway. Translate each operator in turn: ⋈ with a condition = “there exists”, π = “the did of”, − = “but not”. Composing them gives “doctors for whom there is no patient at least as old”, which is “older than all”.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: The relational algebra operator that returns a relation containing only a chosen subset of the attributes of its input is
options: σ (select)
π (projection)
ρ (rename)
⋈ (join)

solution.concept: The six primitive operators act on different aspects of a relation: σ on rows, π on columns, ρ on names, and ×, ∪, − on whole relations.
steps: σ<sub>condition</sub>(R) keeps the rows that satisfy the condition, leaving the schema unchanged.
π<sub>attr list</sub>(R) keeps the listed columns and discards the rest, leaving the rows filtered by duplicate elimination.
ρ renames a relation or its attributes; ⋈ combines two relations on a condition.
solution.trap: σ and π are swapped. A quick check: σ for select rows (horizontal cut), π for project columns (vertical cut).

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The six primitive operators act on different aspects of a relation: σ on rows, π on columns, ρ on names, and ×, ∪, − on whole relations.

Step by step.

  1. σcondition(R) keeps the rows that satisfy the condition, leaving the schema unchanged.
  2. πattr list(R) keeps the listed columns and discards the rest, leaving the rows filtered by duplicate elimination.
  3. ρ renames a relation or its attributes; ⋈ combines two relations on a condition.

Answer: Option (B) — π (projection).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) selects rows, not columns.
  • (C) only changes names.
  • (D) combines two relations.

Common misconception. σ and π are swapped. A quick check: σ for select rows (horizontal cut), π for project columns (vertical cut).

Takeaway. Picture the table: a horizontal cut removes rows (σ), a vertical cut removes columns (π).

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: Let R(A, B) and S(A, B) be union-compatible relations. Which of the following are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: R ∪ S contains every tuple that appears in R or in S or in both, with duplicates removed.
R ∩ S can be written as R − (R − S).
R − S = S − R for all R and S.
R × S contains |R| + |S| tuples.

solution.concept: Set semantics. Union, intersection and difference behave as ordinary set operations once the schemas match; the Cartesian product multiplies cardinalities.
steps: (A) is the definition of set union; since the result is a relation, duplicates collapse.
(B) R − S removes from R everything shared with S; removing those again from R leaves exactly the common part, so R − (R − S) = R ∩ S.
(C) fails for any unequal pair, e.g. R = {t₁}, S = {t₂}.
(D) is wrong: |R × S| = |R| · |S|.
solution.trap: Intersection is thought to need its own operator. It does not: ∩ is derivable from − (and from ⋈). Similarly ∪ is derivable from − and ×, which is why only six operators are primitive.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Set semantics. Union, intersection and difference behave as ordinary set operations once the schemas match; the Cartesian product multiplies cardinalities.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is the definition of set union; since the result is a relation, duplicates collapse.
  2. (B) R − S removes from R everything shared with S; removing those again from R leaves exactly the common part, so R − (R − S) = R ∩ S.
  3. (C) fails for any unequal pair, e.g. R = {t₁}, S = {t₂}.
  4. (D) is wrong: |R × S| = |R| · |S|.

Answer: Options (A) and (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (C) Difference is directional.
  • (D) The Cartesian product multiplies, it does not add.

Common misconception. Intersection is thought to need its own operator. It does not: ∩ is derivable from − (and from ⋈). Similarly ∪ is derivable from − and ×, which is why only six operators are primitive.

Takeaway. Memorise the derivations: R ∩ S = R − (R − S), and |R × S| = |R| × |S|.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question:
Relation R(A, B, C) has 10 tuples and relation S(C, D) has 8 tuples, with C the only common attribute. The tuples of R use exactly 4 distinct values of C, and the tuples of S use exactly 5 distinct values of C. What is the maximum possible number of tuples in R ⋈ S?
(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: The size of a natural join is Σ<sub>c</sub> r_c · s_c over the common attribute, where r_c and s_c are the multiplicities of c in R and S. Under fixed totals the sum of products is largest when the two distributions are aligned and as concentrated as the distinct-value counts allow.
steps: Let r_c ≥ 1 for 4 values of C with Σ r_c = 10, and s_c ≥ 1 for 5 values of C with Σ s_c = 8. Then |R ⋈ S| = Σ_c r_c · s_c.
Because there are 4 and 5 distinct values, at least 1 tuple must be spent on each of them. That leaves 10 − 4 = 6 extra R-tuples and 8 − 5 = 3 extra S-tuples to concentrate on one shared value c₀.
Put all the extras on c₀: r = (7, 1, 1, 1) and s = (4, 1, 1, 1, 1).
Matching the largest counts together gives 7 × 4 = 28 on c₀, and the three remaining shared values contribute 1 × 1 each: 28 + 3 = 31.
No other distribution does better — by the rearrangement inequality the best alignment pairs the largest r_c with the largest s_c, and concentrating mass maximises the largest product.
solution.trap: Multiplying the totals, 10 × 8 = 80, or the distinct counts, 4 × 5 = 20. Both ignore the hard constraint that each of the distinct values must carry at least one tuple.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The size of a natural join is Σc r_c · s_c over the common attribute, where r_c and s_c are the multiplicities of c in R and S. Under fixed totals the sum of products is largest when the two distributions are aligned and as concentrated as the distinct-value counts allow.

Step by step.

  1. Let r_c ≥ 1 for 4 values of C with Σ r_c = 10, and s_c ≥ 1 for 5 values of C with Σ s_c = 8. Then |R ⋈ S| = Σ_c r_c · s_c.
  2. Because there are 4 and 5 distinct values, at least 1 tuple must be spent on each of them. That leaves 10 − 4 = 6 extra R-tuples and 8 − 5 = 3 extra S-tuples to concentrate on one shared value c₀.
  3. Put all the extras on c₀: r = (7, 1, 1, 1) and s = (4, 1, 1, 1, 1).
  4. Matching the largest counts together gives 7 × 4 = 28 on c₀, and the three remaining shared values contribute 1 × 1 each: 28 + 3 = 31.
  5. No other distribution does better — by the rearrangement inequality the best alignment pairs the largest r_c with the largest s_c, and concentrating mass maximises the largest product.

Answer: 31.

Common misconception. Multiplying the totals, 10 × 8 = 80, or the distinct counts, 4 × 5 = 20. Both ignore the hard constraint that each of the distinct values must carry at least one tuple.

Takeaway. Subtract the compulsory one tuple per distinct value first; only the leftovers can be concentrated. Here 6 and 3 leftovers give 7 × 4 = 28 plus 3 forced unit products.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: The tuple relational calculus query { t | t ∈ Student ∧ t[age] > 20 } is equivalent to
options: π_age(σ_age>20(Student))
σ_age>20(Student)
σ_age>20(π_age(Student))
Student ⋈ σ_age>20(Student)

solution.concept: In tuple calculus the free tuple variable ranges over all tuples of the relation named in the membership clause; a conjunctive condition on its attributes corresponds exactly to selection, and no projection is involved because t carries all attributes.
steps: t ∈ Student fixes the range of t to the tuples of Student.
t[age] > 20 is the selection predicate.
The result keeps whole tuples, so the algebra translation is σ_age>20(Student) with the same schema.
Projection would be needed only if the query returned t[some attributes], not t itself.
solution.trap: Students add a projection because the predicate mentions age. The predicate filters; it does not change the output schema. Only an explicit attribute list on t changes the schema.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. In tuple calculus the free tuple variable ranges over all tuples of the relation named in the membership clause; a conjunctive condition on its attributes corresponds exactly to selection, and no projection is involved because t carries all attributes.

Step by step.

  1. t ∈ Student fixes the range of t to the tuples of Student.
  2. t[age] > 20 is the selection predicate.
  3. The result keeps whole tuples, so the algebra translation is σ_age>20(Student) with the same schema.
  4. Projection would be needed only if the query returned t[some attributes], not t itself.

Answer: Option (B) — σ_age>20(Student).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) changes the schema to a single column, which the query does not ask for.
  • (C) projects before selecting, which may drop attributes the predicate needs.
  • (D) joins Student with itself; the calculus query has one variable.

Common misconception. Students add a projection because the predicate mentions age. The predicate filters; it does not change the output schema. Only an explicit attribute list on t changes the schema.

Takeaway. Membership clause → which relation. Conditions on attributes → σ. t[list] on the left of the bar → π of that list.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: In tuple relational calculus, the expression { t | ¬(t ∈ R) } is rejected as unsafe because
options: it is syntactically invalid.
it can denote an infinite relation, since t may take values outside the active domain.
negation is not permitted in relational calculus.
t is a free variable.

solution.concept: A calculus expression is safe when every value it can produce comes from the active domain — the set of values actually occurring in the database. { t | ¬(t ∈ R) } ranges over the infinite universe of all possible tuples, so it is not a finite relation and cannot be evaluated.
steps: The comprehension { t | ¬(t ∈ R) } admits every tuple not in R, over every possible attribute domain.
That set is infinite (or at least unbounded), so it is not a relation in the database sense.
Safety requires each answer tuple to be drawn from dom(R) extended by constants in the query.
Negation itself is perfectly legal — only its unrestricted use is the problem.
solution.final: Option (B) — it can denote an infinite relation
solution.trap: Negation is blamed. The calculus allows ¬ freely; what it forbids is a query whose result is not confined to the active domain. { t | t ∈ R ∧ ¬P(t) } is safe, { t | ¬(t ∈ R) } is not.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A calculus expression is safe when every value it can produce comes from the active domain — the set of values actually occurring in the database. { t | ¬(t ∈ R) } ranges over the infinite universe of all possible tuples, so it is not a finite relation and cannot be evaluated.

Step by step.

  1. The comprehension { t | ¬(t ∈ R) } admits every tuple not in R, over every possible attribute domain.
  2. That set is infinite (or at least unbounded), so it is not a relation in the database sense.
  3. Safety requires each answer tuple to be drawn from dom(R) extended by constants in the query.
  4. Negation itself is perfectly legal — only its unrestricted use is the problem.

Answer: Option (B) — it can denote an infinite relation.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) The syntax is well formed.
  • (C) Negation is allowed; unsafe negation is not.
  • (D) t is free by design — the free variable names the answer tuples.

Common misconception. Negation is blamed. The calculus allows ¬ freely; what it forbids is a query whose result is not confined to the active domain. { t | t ∈ R ∧ ¬P(t) } is safe, { t | ¬(t ∈ R) } is not.

Takeaway. Ask of every calculus query: which relation bounds the free variable? If nothing does, the query is unsafe.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: Which of the following statements about relational calculus are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Tuple relational calculus and domain relational calculus have the same expressive power.
Every relational algebra expression can be written as a safe relational calculus expression.
Relational calculus is procedural: it states how the answer is to be computed.
The safety condition confines a query's values to the active domain of the database.

solution.concept: Relational algebra and the two calculi are all relationally complete: the algebra is procedural, the calculi are declarative, and all three express exactly the same class of queries once safety is imposed.
steps: (A) TRC and DRC are inter-translatable, so neither is more expressive — true.
(B) Codd's theorem gives translations both ways between algebra and safe calculus — true.
(C) Calculus says what the answer is (a set of tuples satisfying a formula); the algebra says how. So calculus is declarative, not procedural.
(D) Safety restricts quantifiers and free variables to the active domain, which is what makes the expression finite — true.
solution.trap: Calculus is assumed to be the “stronger” formalism. In fact it has exactly the same power as the algebra; what it lacks is a fixed evaluation order, which is why SQL compilers translate to algebra.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Relational algebra and the two calculi are all relationally complete: the algebra is procedural, the calculi are declarative, and all three express exactly the same class of queries once safety is imposed.

Step by step.

  1. (A) TRC and DRC are inter-translatable, so neither is more expressive — true.
  2. (B) Codd's theorem gives translations both ways between algebra and safe calculus — true.
  3. (C) Calculus says what the answer is (a set of tuples satisfying a formula); the algebra says how. So calculus is declarative, not procedural.
  4. (D) Safety restricts quantifiers and free variables to the active domain, which is what makes the expression finite — true.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (C) reverses the definitions — calculus is declarative, not procedural.

Common misconception. Calculus is assumed to be the “stronger” formalism. In fact it has exactly the same power as the algebra; what it lacks is a fixed evaluation order, which is why SQL compilers translate to algebra.

Takeaway. Two things to keep straight: procedural = algebra, declarative = calculus, equal in power; and safety is the condition that makes calculus finite.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question:
Let R(A, B) = {(1, 5), (2, 5), (2, 7), (3, 5), (4, 9)}. The domain relational calculus query
{ ⟨a⟩ | ∃b (⟨a, b⟩ ∈ R ∧ b = 5) }
returns how many distinct values of a?
(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: A domain-calculus query projects the free variables of its formula. The existential quantifier on b makes b a bound (projected-away) variable, so the answer is the set of a-values that co-occur with b = 5.
steps: The formula requires a pair (a, b) in R with b = 5.
Pairs with b = 5 are (1, 5), (2, 5) and (3, 5).
Their a-values are 1, 2, 3 — three distinct values.
(2, 7) and (4, 9) are excluded because their b is not 5.
In algebra this is π_A(σ_B=5(R)), which has 3 tuples.
solution.trap: Counting tuples rather than distinct a-values, or being distracted by the repeated a = 2. The result of a calculus query is a set, so a = 2 contributes once.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A domain-calculus query projects the free variables of its formula. The existential quantifier on b makes b a bound (projected-away) variable, so the answer is the set of a-values that co-occur with b = 5.

Step by step.

  1. The formula requires a pair (a, b) in R with b = 5.
  2. Pairs with b = 5 are (1, 5), (2, 5) and (3, 5).
  3. Their a-values are 1, 2, 3 — three distinct values.
  4. (2, 7) and (4, 9) are excluded because their b is not 5.
  5. In algebra this is π_A(σ_B=5(R)), which has 3 tuples.

Answer: 3.

Common misconception. Counting tuples rather than distinct a-values, or being distracted by the repeated a = 2. The result of a calculus query is a set, so a = 2 contributes once.

Takeaway. Free variables = output columns. Here only a is free, so translate to π_A(σ_B=5(R)) and count.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: Which one of the following queries cannot be expressed in relational algebra, nor in safe relational calculus?
options: Names of employees who earn more than their manager.
Names of all employees who are, directly or indirectly, subordinates of a given employee.
Names of employees who work on every project.
Names of employees who work on no project.

solution.concept: Relational algebra and safe calculus are relationally complete but not Turing complete: they can express any finite first-order query over the stored relations, and nothing that needs an unbounded number of iteration steps. Transitive closure is the standard query outside that class.

questions.question: Entity sets A (m entities) and B (n entities), with m, n ≥ 1, take part in a many-to-many relationship R, and both participations are total. The number of tuples in the relation that represents R lies
options: exactly at m · n.
between max(m, n) and m · n, inclusive.
between m + n and m · n, inclusive.
exactly at m + n.

solution.concept: Two independent constraints bound a many-to-many relationship: the ratio gives the upper bound and total participation gives the lower bound.
steps: Upper bound: each of the m A-entities may pair with each of the n B-entities, so at most m · n distinct pairs.
Lower bound from A's side: total participation means every A-entity appears in at least one pair, so at least m pairs.
Lower bound from B's side: every B-entity appears in at least one pair, so at least n pairs.
Pairs are distinct tuples, so the count is at least the larger of the two bounds, i.e. at least max(m, n). Both bounds are attainable.
Hence max(m, n) ≤ |R| ≤ m · n.
solution.trap: Adding the cardinalities (m + n) or assuming the maximum is forced. The maximum m · n needs every A-entity to pair with every B-entity, which the m:n ratio permits but does not require.

questions.question: W is a weak entity set owned by entity set E through the identifying relationship R. Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

The participation of W in R is total.
The primary key of the relation built from W is the primary key of E together with W's partial key.
A W-entity may exist without being related to any E-entity.

(D) contradicts existence dependency: an owner-less weak entity has no identity at all — so (D) is false.

questions.question:
An ER schema contains entity sets A, B, C, D; a weak entity set W owned by A; a multivalued attribute phone on B; a 1:N relationship from A to C; a many-to-many relationship between B and D; and a ternary relationship among A, B and C.
Applying the standard ER-to-relational mapping — one relation per strong or weak entity set, a separate relation per multivalued attribute, a 1:N relationship absorbed into the relation on its many side, and a separate relation per m:n or n-ary relationship — how many relations does the schema produce?

solution.concept: The ER-to-relational mapping is a fixed recipe; the question is which constructs cost a relation and which are absorbed into an existing one.
steps: Strong entity sets A, B, C, D → 4 relations.
Weak entity set W → 1 more relation (it becomes a relation whose key is A's key plus W's partial key) → 5.
Multivalued attribute phone → 1 more relation (owner key + phone value) → 6.
1:N relationship A → C → 0 new relations; it is absorbed as a foreign key in C → still 6.
m:n relationship B–D → 1 more relation → 7.
Ternary relationship among A, B, C → 1 more relation → 8.
solution.trap: Charging a relation for the 1:N relationship, or forgetting that a weak entity set still gets its own relation. The 1:N side is the free one; the weak entity set is not.

questions.question: Which one of the following statements about a ternary relationship R among entity sets A, B and C is TRUE?
options: R is always equivalent to three binary relationships among A, B and C.
R can record a combination of an A-entity, a B-entity and a C-entity that no collection of binary relationships can record.
R must be many-to-many in all three directions.
R requires every entity to take part exactly once.

solution.concept: A relationship of degree three is an association among three entities simultaneously, not three associations among pairs.
steps: A ternary relationship instance is a triple (a, b, c).

Three binary relationships would instead store (a, b), (b, c) and (a, c) separately. From those three pairs you cannot tell which triples actually occurred: the pairs (a1, b1), (b1, c1), (a1, c1) are consistent with both (a1, b1, c1) and with (a1, b1, c2), (a1, b2, c1), …
So the ternary relationship carries information the binary decomposition loses — (B) is true and (A) is false.
Nothing forces the ratio to be m:n in every direction, and nothing forces single participation — (C) and (D) are false.
solution.trap: Assuming a ternary relationship is just 'three binary ones glued together'. It is not, and that is precisely why the ER-to-relational mapping gives an n-ary relationship its own relation.

questions.question: Entity set A has a one-to-many relationship R with entity set B — that is, one A-entity is related to many B-entities. Which statement is TRUE?
options: Each B-entity is related to at most one A-entity.
Each A-entity is related to at most one B-entity.
Each A-entity must be related to at least one B-entity.
Each B-entity must be related to at least one A-entity.

solution.concept: A cardinality ratio constrains how many entities on one side may be associated with an entity on the other. It says nothing about whether an entity must be associated at all — that is participation, a separate constraint.

questions.question: Relation R(A, B, C, D, E) satisfies the functional dependencies F = {A → B, BC → D, D → E, E → C}. The number of candidate keys of R is

solution.concept: A candidate key is a minimal attribute set whose closure is all five attributes. Enumerate closures, then drop any set that contains a smaller key.
steps: A⁺ = {A, B} — BC → D needs C, so nothing further fires. A alone is not a key.
{A, C}⁺: A → B adds B; BC → D adds D; D → E adds E. Closure is all five — {A, C} is a key.
{A, D}⁺: A → B; D → E; E → C; then BC → D. All five — {A, D} is a key.
{A, E}⁺: A → B; E → C; BC → D; D → E. All five — {A, E} is a key.
No set without A closes: from {B, C, D, E} the rules BC → D, D → E, E → C never produce A.
So the candidate keys are {A, C}, {A, D}, {A, E} — three, all minimal.
solution.trap: Stopping at the first key found, or counting {A, C, D} as a fourth key. A superset of a key is a superkey, never a candidate key.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about functional dependencies are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: A → B is trivial exactly when B ⊆ A.
If A → B and B → C, then A → C.
If A → B, then AC → BC for every attribute set C.
If A → B and C → B, then A → C.

solution.concept: Armstrong's axioms: reflexivity, augmentation and transitivity generate every dependency implied by a set, and nothing else does.
steps: Reflexivity: A → B holds automatically when B ⊆ A, because a set always determines its own subsets. Such a dependency is called trivial — (A) is true.
Transitivity: A → B and B → C give A → C — (B) is true.
Augmentation: adding the same attributes to both sides preserves the dependency, so A → B yields AC → BC — (C) is true.
(D) is the converse of transitivity and is not a valid rule. Two different sets may each determine B without determining each other — (D) is false.
solution.trap: Treating A → B, C → B ⊢ A → C as transitivity. Transitivity needs the same set on the right of one dependency and the left of the next; here the shared attribute is on the right of both.

Two tuples that agree on a non-key attribute.

questions.question: Consider Works(eid, pid) and Projects(pid). Which expressions return exactly the eids of employees who work on every project? (Select all that apply.)
options: πeid(Works) ÷ πpid(Projects)
πeid(Works) − πeid((πeid(Works) × πpid(Projects)) − Works)
πeid(Works) − πeid(πeid(Works) × πpid(Projects))
πeid(Works ⋈ Projects)

solution.concept: 'For all' is division. Equivalently, it is 'difference of difference': take everyone, subtract those who miss at least one project.
steps: (A) is the division operator applied directly: it returns the eids whose set of projects contains the whole of πpid(Projects) — true.
(B) builds the set of missing pairs — every (eid, pid) combination that is not in Works — projects it to eid, and subtracts it from all employees. What survives misses no project — true.
(C) subtracts all employees who work on anything at all, which returns only employees with no project — false.
(D) returns every employee who works on at least one project — that is 'exists', not 'for all' — false.
solution.trap: Reading (D) as the answer. A join with the projects relation answers 'works on some project'; the universal quantifier needs division or the double difference.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. 'For all' is division. Equivalently, it is 'difference of difference': take everyone, subtract those who miss at least one project.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is the division operator applied directly: it returns the eids whose set of projects contains the whole of πpid(Projects) — true.
  2. (B) builds the set of missing pairs — every (eid, pid) combination that is not in Works — projects it to eid, and subtracts it from all employees. What survives misses no project — true.
  3. (C) subtracts all employees who work on anything at all, which returns only employees with no project — false.
  4. (D) returns every employee who works on at least one project — that is 'exists', not 'for all' — false.

Answer: Options (A) and (B).

Common misconception. Reading (D) as the answer. A join with the projects relation answers 'works on some project'; the universal quantifier needs division or the double difference.

questions.question: Let S(B) be a relation with zero tuples. For a relation R(A, B), the division R ÷ S is
options: the empty relation.
πA(R).
undefined, because division needs a non-empty divisor.
R.

solution.concept: Division asks: which A-values are paired with every B-value in S? With an empty S the requirement is vacuously satisfied by every value.
steps: By definition, R ÷ S = { a | for every b ∈ S, (a, b) ∈ R }.
When S = ∅ there is no b to check, so the condition holds for every a that appears in R.
The values of a that appear in R are exactly πA(R), so R ÷ ∅ = πA(R).
Confirm with the derived formula: πA(R) − πA((πA(R) × ∅) − R) = πA(R) − πA(∅) = πA(R).
solution.trap: Answering 'the empty relation' by pattern-matching 'empty input, empty output'. Universally quantified conditions are vacuously true over an empty range, so the result is the largest possible set, not the smallest.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

  3. The values of a that appear in R are exactly πA(R), so R ÷ ∅ = πA(R).

questions.question: Let R(A, B) and S(B, C), where B is a key of R and a foreign key in S that is never NULL. Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: R ⋈ S has exactly as many tuples as S.
R ⋈ S has attributes A, B and C.
R ⋈ S can contain more tuples than |R| × |S|.
The natural join is associative.

solution.concept: A natural join equates the common attributes and keeps one copy of each. When the common attribute is a key on one side, the join is a lookup, not a product.
steps: Every tuple of S has a non-NULL B-value, and referential integrity guarantees a matching R-tuple. Since B is a key of R, that partner is unique — one joined tuple per S-tuple, so the counts are equal — (A) is true.
The common attribute appears once, and the remaining attributes of both sides are retained — (B) is true.
A join can never produce more than the Cartesian product |R| × |S|; it selects a subset of those pairs — (C) is false.
(R ⋈ S) ⋈ T = R ⋈ (S ⋈ T) for natural joins, and it is commutative too — (D) is true.
solution.trap: Believing a natural join can blow up the row count. Duplication on the common attribute is what multiplies rows, and a key on one side makes that impossible.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A natural join equates the common attributes and keeps one copy of each. When the common attribute is a key on one side, the join is a lookup, not a product.

Step by step.

  1. Every tuple of S has a non-NULL B-value, and referential integrity guarantees a matching R-tuple. Since B is a key of R, that partner is unique — one joined tuple per S-tuple, so the counts are equal — (A) is true.
  2. The common attribute appears once, and the remaining attributes of both sides are retained — (B) is true.
  3. A join can never produce more than the Cartesian product |R| × |S|; it selects a subset of those pairs — (C) is false.
  4. (R ⋈ S) ⋈ T = R ⋈ (S ⋈ T) for natural joins, and it is commutative too — (D) is true.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

questions.question: Relations R(A, B) and S(A, B) are union-compatible, with |R| = 12, |S| = 9 and |R − S| = 5. The number of tuples in R ∩ S is

solution.concept: R splits into two disjoint parts: the tuples it shares with S, and the tuples it does not.
steps: R = (R − S) ∪ (R ∩ S), and the two parts are disjoint.
So |R| = |R − S| + |R ∩ S|.
Substituting: 12 = 5 + |R ∩ S|, hence |R ∩ S| = 7.
solution.trap: Using |R ∪ S| instead: that would give 12 + 9 − 7 = 14, a different quantity. The stated set is the difference, not the union.

  3. Substituting: 12 = 5 + |R ∩ S|, hence |R ∩ S| = 7.

free.
quantified over the domain of A.
unsafe.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the domain relational calculus are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: A query has the form { ⟨x₁, …, xₙ⟩ | P(x₁, …, xₙ) }.
Its variables range over domain values rather than over whole tuples.
Safety confines the result to values drawn from the active domain.
It is strictly more expressive than relational algebra.

solution.concept: Domain calculus is the value-based counterpart of tuple calculus: the variables are single values, and the result is a set of value-tuples.
steps: The result is a set of value-tuples ⟨x₁, …, xₙ⟩ satisfying P — (A) is true.
Each xᵢ ranges over the domain of an attribute, not over tuples — that is the distinction from tuple calculus — (B) is true.
Safety restricts every variable to the active domain — the set of values actually occurring in the database — which is what makes the result finite — (C) is true.
Domain calculus, tuple calculus and relational algebra are all equivalent in expressive power (Codd's theorem), so (D) is false.
solution.trap: Believing one calculus is stronger than the other. Both are exactly as strong as relational algebra — and all three fall short of transitive closure.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Step by step.

  1. The result is a set of value-tuples ⟨x₁, …, xₙ⟩ satisfying P — (A) is true.
  2. Each xᵢ ranges over the domain of an attribute, not over tuples — that is the distinction from tuple calculus — (B) is true.

  4. Domain calculus, tuple calculus and relational algebra are all equivalent in expressive power (Codd's theorem), so (D) is false.

questions.question: Let R(A, B) = {(1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 1), (4, 2), (5, 3)}. The number of tuples in { ⟨a₁, a₂⟩ | ∃b (R(a₁, b) ∧ R(a₂, b) ∧ a₁ ≠ a₂) } is

solution.concept: The shared bound variable b links two occurrences of the same relation — a self-join expressed in calculus. The condition a₁ ≠ a₂ removes the diagonal.
steps: Group the tuples by b.
b = 2: a ∈ {1, 4} → the ordered pairs (1, 4) and (4, 1) → 2.
b = 3: a ∈ {2, 5} → (2, 5) and (5, 2) → 2.
b = 1: a ∈ {3} only → no pair with a₁ ≠ a₂ → 0.
Total 2 + 2 + 0 = 4.
solution.trap: Forgetting that the answer is ordered. ⟨a₁, a₂⟩ and ⟨a₂, a₁⟩ are different tuples, so {1, 4} contributes two, not one. Dropping the a₁ ≠ a₂ condition would add the three diagonal tuples.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The shared bound variable b links two occurrences of the same relation — a self-join expressed in calculus. The condition a₁ ≠ a₂ removes the diagonal.

Step by step.

  1. Group the tuples by b.
  2. b = 2: a ∈ {1, 4} → the ordered pairs (1, 4) and (4, 1) → 2.
  3. b = 3: a ∈ {2, 5} → (2, 5) and (5, 2) → 2.
  4. b = 1: a ∈ {3} only → no pair with a₁ ≠ a₂ → 0.
  5. Total 2 + 2 + 0 = 4.

Answer: 4

Common misconception. Forgetting that the answer is ordered. ⟨a₁, a₂⟩ and ⟨a₂, a₁⟩ are different tuples, so {1, 4} contributes two, not one. Dropping the a₁ ≠ a₂ condition would add the three diagonal tuples.

questions.question: For union-compatible R(A, B) and S(A, B), which tuple calculus expression is equivalent to R − S?
options: { t | t ∈ R ∧ ¬(t ∈ S) }
{ t | ¬(t ∈ R) ∧ t ∈ S }
{ t | t ∈ R ∨ t ∈ S }
{ t | ¬(t ∈ R ∧ t ∈ S) }

(B) is S − R, the other difference.
(C) is R ∪ S.
(D) is the complement of the intersection — everything except the shared tuples.
solution.trap: Swapping the operands: t ∈ R ∧ ¬(t ∈ S) and ¬(t ∈ R) ∧ t ∈ S look symmetric but are different sets. Order matters in difference.

questions.solution_html:

Step by step.

  1. 'In R and not in S' translates to t ∈ R ∧ ¬(t ∈ S) — (A).
  2. (B) is S − R, the other difference.
  3. (C) is R ∪ S.
  4. (D) is the complement of the intersection — everything except the shared tuples.
